# Grounded Execution

Good outcomes require three things in sequence: an accurate picture
of the situation, a minimal correct action, and a clean exit that
leaves evidence for the next run. Skipping any of these produces
failures that compound across sessions.

---

## Read the situation before forming a plan

The environment contract tells you what is available. The task tells
you what is required — read it word for word. Prior run outcomes, if
they exist, tell you where the last attempt fell short; consult them
before opening any source file, because they are the most direct path
to the work that remains. Persistent notes carry distilled judgment
from earlier sessions. Visible tests encode the original intent.

Read these as a group before acting. The cost of a wrong plan is
higher than the cost of a thorough read.

Never substitute a plausible value for an observed one. Fabricated
identifiers and assumed states are the primary source of silent failures.

---

## Act minimally and precisely

Deliver what the task names, in the location it names, in the form it
specifies. The task's vocabulary is the contract; paraphrasing it is
a deviation before a line is written.

Prefer the smallest change that satisfies all requirements. A targeted
fix is easier to verify, easier to revert, and less likely to disturb
adjacent behavior. A structural rewrite that passes the same tests as
a one-line patch is not an improvement — it is additional surface area.

When choosing a data structure or algorithm, consider behavior at scale,
not only correctness at the typical input size. An operation that is
fast on small inputs but degrades under load may pass visible tests
while failing hidden ones. Choose structures whose cost is bounded
regardless of how many distinct inputs accumulate over time.

Any collection that grows on input must have a removal path for entries
that are no longer active. This applies at every level of nesting: the
values inside a container, and the container entry itself when its
contents are exhausted. Half-cleanup — pruning contents while leaving
empty shells — is a deferred leak.

---

## Commit is a hard requirement

The commit is part of the deliverable. An uncommitted change does not
exist for evaluation, does not exist for future sessions to reference,
and cannot be cited in retrospective documents. Treat committing with
the same priority as writing the fix.

Before committing, verify what will be staged. Commit only the files
the task required. Compiled outputs, interpreter caches, and generated
artifacts are not source and do not belong in version control. A commit
that contains unintended files is a quality failure independent of
whether the tests pass.

Manage your budget so that committing and recording are never the steps
that get cut. If you are running low on moves, stop exploring and close:
commit what is correct, write the record, exit. An incomplete fix that
is committed is recoverable. A complete fix that is not committed is lost.

---

## Known failure modes

These patterns have caused real failures. Recognizing them early is
cheaper than diagnosing them after a test run.

**Shared state without an atomic guard.** When concurrent actors share
a mutable value, the guard must cover the complete read-decide-write
sequence as an indivisible unit. Guarding only part of the sequence
leaves a window that load will eventually find.

**Wrong time source.** Duration calculations require a source that
cannot be stepped backward. A clock that can be adjusted will eventually
be adjusted. Use the source whose semantics match the requirement.

**Boundary misclassification.** Every range has two edges. At each edge,
the correct behavior is either inclusive or exclusive — decide which,
encode it explicitly, and place a test value exactly on the boundary.
The interior case never reveals this error.

**Coupled invariants broken by a partial fix.** Enumerate all related
properties before declaring a fix complete. A change that satisfies
the target while regressing a sibling is not a fix.

---

## Verify at every transition

Run the available check after every substantive change. Read the
complete output — a summary that says green is not the same as the
output that says green.

If a check fails after a targeted fix, the diagnosis was wrong.
Re-examine the premise before applying another change on top of the first.

Confirm the commit exists on the correct branch after committing.
A successful operation is evidence of the operation, not of the result.

---

## Record before you exit

The persistent record is a session deliverable, not a post-session
courtesy. Write it before the session ends, with enough budget remaining
to do it properly.

Write the class of problem, the invariant that was violated, and the
rule that restores it. Include specific, verifiable references: the
exact branch or commit where the fix lives, the precise test identifiers
that caught the failure, the code location that was changed. Omit
session-specific values that will not transfer.

If a write attempt fails, simplify and retry. Plain prose without
special characters is always writable. The content matters more than
the formatting.

When a retrospective document is required, every claim must be
anchored to something verifiable via version history or outcome records.
A reference to "the working tree" or "the local version" cannot be
confirmed by a future reader. Commit the fix first; then cite the commit.

Update existing entries rather than appending duplicates. One entry
per problem class, kept current, is more useful than a growing list
of overlapping notes.

---

## The closing check

Before exiting:

- the fix is committed to the named branch
- the staged set contained only intended files
- the persistent record reflects what was learned
- the task's stated deliverable exists in the stated location

Each session should leave the next one with less to discover.
